CALIFORNIA'S ANTI-SLAPP STATUTE IN CONFIDENTIALITY/IP DISPUTES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS ANTI-SLAPP INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's anti-SLAPP statute, Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16, and summarizes how published California case law has addressed its application to confidentiality, trade secret, and other intellectual-property-related claims. It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning a matter involving Acme, Inc. and Beta Corp. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing what the statute says and how courts have construed it; it does not determine whether any specific claim described in that matter does or does not arise from activity protected under the statute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE ANTI-SLAPP STATUTE: PURPOSE AND THE SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE
Code of Civil Procedure section 425.16 is California's anti-SLAPP statute (SLAPP stands for Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation). Subdivision (a) states the Legislature's finding that there has been a disturbing increase in lawsuits brought primarily to chill the valid exercise of the constitutional rights of freedom of speech and petition, and directs that the section be construed broadly to encourage continued participation in matters of public significance. The statute creates a "special motion to strike" that a defendant may bring against a cause of action arising from the defendant's protected petitioning or free-speech activity. The motion must generally be filed within 60 days of service of the complaint, though the court has discretion to permit a later filing on terms it deems proper, and the clerk must schedule a hearing not more than 30 days after the motion is served unless docket conditions require a later date. Filing the motion automatically stays all discovery in the action until the court rules on the motion, subject to the court's authority to order specified discovery to proceed on a noticed motion and for good cause shown. An order granting or denying a special motion to strike is itself immediately appealable.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The Legislature finds and declares that it is in the public interest to encourage continued participation in matters of public significance, and that this participation should not be chilled through abuse of the judicial process. To this end, this section shall be construed broadly."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(a), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)
  "The special motion may be filed within 60 days of the service of the complaint or, in the court’s discretion, at any later time upon terms it deems proper. The motion shall be scheduled by the clerk of the court for a hearing not more than 30 days after the service of the motion unless the docket conditions of the court require a later hearing."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(f), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(f) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)
  "All discovery proceedings in the action shall be stayed upon the filing of a notice of motion made pursuant to this section. The stay of discovery shall remain in effect until notice of entry of the order ruling on the motion."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(g), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)

The statute text quoted reflects the version as amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 444, Sec. 1 (SB 577), effective January 1, 2025, per the amendment note appended to the statute text on the official site.

THE TWO-STEP ANALYSIS COURTS APPLY TO A SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE
Subdivision (b)(1) of section 425.16 states the statute's core operative rule: a cause of action arising from a person's act in furtherance of that person's right of petition or free speech in connection with a public issue is subject to a special motion to strike, unless the court determines the plaintiff has established a probability of prevailing on the claim. Published California case law construing this subdivision describes it as a two-step (or two-prong) analysis. At the first step, the defendant bringing the motion has the burden of showing that the challenged cause of action arises from protected activity, as defined in subdivision (e). If the defendant makes that showing, the analysis moves to the second step, at which the burden shifts to the plaintiff to demonstrate a probability of prevailing on the claim; subdivision (b)(2) directs the court to consider the pleadings and supporting and opposing affidavits stating the facts on which liability or a defense is based in making that determination. If the plaintiff does not carry that burden, the claim is stricken. Subdivision (b)(3) further provides that a finding the plaintiff has established a probability of prevailing is not itself admissible at a later stage of the case or in a subsequent action, and does not affect any burden or degree of proof otherwise applicable later in the case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A cause of action against a person arising from any act of that person in furtherance of the person’s right of petition or free speech under the United States Constitution or the California Constitution in connection with a public issue shall be subject to a special motion to strike, unless the court determines that the plaintiff has established that there is a probability that the plaintiff will prevail on the claim."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(b), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(b)(1)-(3) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)

The description of the mechanism as a "two-step" or "two-prong" analysis is standard terminology used throughout California case law construing this subdivision (including in the case discussed in the case-law clause below, which describes a "first prong" and burden-shifting to the plaintiff); it is not itself statutory text and is not separately cited to a specific opinion in this clause.

THE STATUTORY DEFINITION OF PROTECTED PETITIONING AND FREE SPEECH ACTIVITY
Subdivision (e) of section 425.16 defines the phrase "act in furtherance of a person's right of petition or free speech under the United States or California Constitution in connection with a public issue" to include four categories of conduct: (1) any written or oral statement or writing made before a legislative, executive, or judicial proceeding, or any other official proceeding authorized by law; (2) any written or oral statement or writing made in connection with an issue under consideration or review by a legislative, executive, or judicial body, or any other official proceeding authorized by law; (3) any written or oral statement or writing made in a place open to the public or a public forum in connection with an issue of public interest; and (4) any other conduct in furtherance of the exercise of the constitutional right of petition or the constitutional right of free speech in connection with a public issue or an issue of public interest. Confidentiality- and trade-secret-related disputes that involve anti-SLAPP motions most often implicate the third and fourth categories, since a defendant in that context typically argues that the conduct the plaintiff sues over (a public statement, a business communication, or similar conduct) touched on a public issue or an issue of public interest, rather than arguing the conduct occurred before, or in connection with, an official proceeding.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(e), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(e) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)

The final sentence, describing which categories most often come up in this project's specific subject-matter context (confidentiality/trade secret/IP disputes), is this project's own characterization based on the single case discussed in the case-law clause below, not a statement independently verified across a broader sample of cases.

FEE-SHIFTING CONSEQUENCES OF A SPECIAL MOTION TO STRIKE
Section 425.16 attaches significant fee-shifting consequences to the special motion to strike. Under subdivision (c)(1), except as provided in subdivision (c)(2), a defendant who prevails on a special motion to strike is entitled to recover that defendant's attorney's fees and costs. The same subdivision also runs in the opposite direction: if the court finds that a special motion to strike is frivolous or is solely intended to cause unnecessary delay, the court must award costs and reasonable attorney's fees to a plaintiff who prevails on the motion, pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 128.5. Subdivision (c)(2) carves out certain government-related causes of action (those brought under Government Code sections 11130, 11130.3, 54960, or 54960.1, or under the California Public Records Act provisions commencing with Government Code section 7923.100) from the prevailing defendant's automatic fee entitlement, while preserving other, more specific fee-recovery provisions that may apply to those same causes of action.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "a prevailing defendant on a special motion to strike shall be entitled to recover that defendant’s attorney’s fees and costs. If the court finds that a special motion to strike is frivolous or is solely intended to cause unnecessary delay, the court shall award costs and reasonable attorney’s fees to a plaintiff prevailing on the motion, pursuant to Section 128.5."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 425.16(c)(1), Cal. Civ. Proc. Code § 425.16(c)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=425.16)
  Known gap: Statute text fetched and cross-checked as described in the companion overview clause. This clause states the fee-shifting mechanism generally; it does not address the separate body of California case law on how courts calculate a reasonable fee award under subdivision (c)(1) (for example, lodestar and multiplier methodology), which is outside the scope of this Information Sheet.

CASE LAW: ANTI-SLAPP MOTIONS AGAINST TRADE SECRET AND CONFIDENTIALITY-RELATED CLAIMS
Whether a trade secret misappropriation, breach-of-confidentiality, or related claim qualifies for anti-SLAPP treatment is a fact-intensive question that published California case law resolves by looking to the specific conduct the claim is based on, not the general subject matter of the dispute. In World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., a company sued a competitor and several of its own former sales associates for, among other claims, misappropriation of trade secrets and breach of contract, based on allegations that the defendants used the company's confidential associate and customer lists and other trade secrets to solicit its associates and customers to switch to the competing company. The defendants brought a special motion to strike, arguing that their solicitation activity was protected free speech in connection with a public issue because it involved "the pursuit of lawful employment" and "workforce mobility and free competition." The Court of Appeal rejected that argument and affirmed denial of the motion, holding that the complaint did not arise from protected activity: although employee mobility and competition can be issues of public interest "considered in the abstract," the defendants' actual communications were commercial solicitations of a competitor's employees and customers made for the sole purpose of furthering a business interest, not statements about, or intended to inform the public on, those broader topics. The court explained that the relevant test looks to "the principal thrust or gravamen" of the cause of action, so that allegations of protected activity that are merely incidental to a claim based essentially on nonprotected activity do not bring the claim within the statute, and warned that treating ordinary noncompetition or trade-secret claims as categorically subject to anti-SLAPP motions merely because they touch on employee mobility would improperly extend the statute to swallow the underlying substantive law. This same fact-specific, gravamen-focused approach is the framework California courts have applied more generally to determine whether a trade-secret or confidentiality-related claim is or is not based on protected petitioning or speech activity; the outcome in any given case turns on the specific conduct alleged, not on the mere presence of a business or competitive relationship between the parties.

The trial court denied the motion on the ground that defendants failed to make a prima facie showing that the complaint arose from protected activity. We affirm."
  — World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1561 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist., Apr. 16, 2009, mod. May 7, 2009), 172 Cal.App.4th 1561, 92 Cal.Rptr.3d 227 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2288025/world-financial-group-inc-v-hbw-insurance-financial-services-inc/)
  "Though couched in noble language, defendants’ communications were not “about” these broad topics, nor were they designed to inform the public of an issue of public interest. They were merely solicitations of a competitor’s employees and customers undertaken for the sole purpose of furthering a business interest."
  — World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1561 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist. 2009), 172 Cal.App.4th 1561, 92 Cal.Rptr.3d 227 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2288025/world-financial-group-inc-v-hbw-insurance-financial-services-inc/)

  — World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1561 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist. 2009), 172 Cal.App.4th 1561, 92 Cal.Rptr.3d 227 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2288025/world-financial-group-inc-v-hbw-insurance-financial-services-inc/)
  "Otherwise, every case alleging the breach of a noncompetition agreement or the related misappropriation of trade secrets would be categorically subject to the anti-SLAPP statute."
  — World Financial Group, Inc. v. HBW Insurance & Financial Services, Inc., 172 Cal. App. 4th 1561 (Cal. Ct. App., 2d Dist. 2009), 172 Cal.App.4th 1561, 92 Cal.Rptr.3d 227 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2288025/world-financial-group-inc-v-hbw-insurance-financial-services-inc/)

Because this research was constrained by CourtListener's roughly 50-requests-per-hour rate limit, only this one case was independently read and verified in full. This is genuinely a fact-intensive, mixed body of law: whether a trade-secret or confidentiality claim "arises from" protected activity turns on the specific pleaded conduct (for example, whether the underlying communications were made in an official proceeding or public forum under subdivision (e)(1)-(3), versus ordinary commercial solicitation as in this case), and this single case should not be read as establishing that anti-SLAPP motions against trade secret or confidentiality claims never succeed — only that this particular category of claim (commercial solicitation of a competitor's customers/employees using confidential information) was held not to arise from protected activity on the facts presented here.
